turns.t: I'm grand, doctor, really. It was only Bridget here who insisted I come in for the check on the leg after the tablets.
Good on Bridget, then. This is the second time it's flared up on that shin, so I'd sooner look than guess. Bridget, you're with him at home?
I am, I'm his live-in carer, five days a week. He'd never tell you if it was bad, so I tell you for him.
There's nothing to tell.
Fair enough, we'll see. Is it all right if the healthcare assistant takes down the dressing first?
Hello Mr Doyle. I'll unwrap the leg and have the dressing pack ready for the doctor, it won't take a minute.
Ah, don't be making a fuss.
While she does that, a couple of questions. Any fever or shivers since I last saw you?
No fever.
And any pain in the leg, or is it just a bit tender?
No pain. Nothing worth mentioning.
He doesn't complain, that's the problem. But I'll say he's been walking the garden path every day without limping.
That's useful to hear from you, thank you. Now, the tablets. Which antibiotic are you finishing?
The doxycycline, 100 mg, twice a day. I've two days left.
Good. And you're taking that because of the penicillin trouble, aren't you?
I am. Penicillin gave me hives years ago. They told me never again.
Right, penicillin allergy with hives, I'll make sure that's on the front of your notes. Any other tablets I should know about?
There's the water tablet for the swelling, the furosemide. It's in the morning. I think it's maybe 20 mg? I'd have to check the box.
Maybe 20 mg, we'll confirm it against the pharmacy list. Mr Doyle, do you remember?
I take what Bridget puts in my hand.
Fair. Anything long-term behind the swollen legs?
The heart failure. It's well managed. And I had the hip replaced about ten years ago.
Heart failure and the hip replacement, thank you. Let's have a look at the leg.
Temperature is 36.8 degrees, and your pulse is 76. Now I'm looking at the shin. The redness has faded to a pale pink, and there's no warmth over the skin where it was.
Is that good or bad?
Good. It looks like the cellulitis has cleared, which is what we wanted from this course.
I told you it was nothing.
You did, and I'm still glad we checked. Now let me give you the choices for keeping it from coming back a third time.
Please do. I'm tired of the carpet being covered in cotton wool.

First option, compression stockings in the daytime, which helps the swelling that sets the skin up for infection. Second, moisturise the skin twice a day so it doesn't crack. Third, keep your feet up when you're sitting.
The stockings are a divil to get on.
They are. Bridget or the community nurse can help with that. Which of the three would you actually do?
The moisturiser. I'd do that.
And I'll do the feet up, if I have to tie him to the stool.
Then moisturiser every day, feet up when sitting, and finish the doxycycline. We can talk about the stockings another day.
Grand. Will that be everything?
That's everything for today. You look well, Mr Doyle.
I'll put a light dressing back on, and a clean sock over it.
Thanks, love.
I'll bring him in for a cup of tea first, we passed a lovely bakery.
Enjoy it. Take care, both of you.
Good day, doctor.

chief_complaint.normalized_value: Review of lower leg after cellulitis treatment

clinical_actions.description: Moisturise daily, keep feet up when sitting, finish doxycycline
